name: Dropover
tagline: A macOS utility that lets you shake a drag to drop files into a floating shelf, then drag them out somewhere else later.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The concept is small: a floating window that holds file URLs and acts as both a drag destination and a drag source. An agent fluent in AppKit can get a working shelf up in a session, and for the plain case of dragging Finder files between windows it will feel fine. The pain is everything around the edges: detecting a shake mid-drag without a global event tap misbehaving, accepting lazy file promises from browsers and Photos instead of just file URLs, dragging items back out as real files, and keeping the panel above fullscreen apps without stealing focus. None of that is impossible, it is just a long tail of AppKit trivia that eats the weekend you thought you saved. Call it a working personal shelf, not a replacement for the polish.
coreLoopDIY: A borderless always-on-top panel that accepts dropped files, shows them as a stack, and serves them back as a drag source into any other app.
requirements: Swift and AppKit knowledge for debugging drag sessions
Accessibility or input monitoring permission if you want shake detection
Ad hoc code signing, or a developer account if you want it to run elsewhere
whatYouLose: Reliable shake-to-summon during an active drag, which is the entire reason people bought it
File promise handling, so dragging an image out of Safari or Photos may give you nothing useful
Cloud upload and share links, AirDrop, and share sheet actions from the shelf
Multiple shelves, stacking animations, and the general feel of a thing that never gets in the way
Notarization, auto updates, and someone else fixing it when the next macOS breaks drag APIs
moatNotes: The moat is entirely in the hundred small interaction decisions, plus one developer who has been chasing AppKit drag regressions for years.
whyPeopleStillPay: It is cheap, it is native, and it does one annoying thing perfectly on the first try. Most people who try to rebuild a shelf discover that the hard part is not holding file references, it is making the window appear at the right moment under the cursor without interrupting the drag that is already in flight. Paying once for a utility that already solved that is an easy trade against a weekend of NSDraggingSession documentation.
notes: Great weekend project, mediocre weekend ROI.
prompt:
Build a macOS drag-and-drop shelf utility called Shelf, in Swift with AppKit. No SwiftUI, no cross platform layer.

Scaffold an Xcode project in this folder using XcodeGen with a project.yml. Target macOS 14 or later. Set LSUIElement to true so there is no Dock icon. Disable the app sandbox so the app can read arbitrary dropped file URLs.

In scope:
- A menu bar item with: Show Shelf, Clear Shelf, Quit.
- A borderless NSPanel, level .floating, canJoinAllSpaces plus fullScreenAuxiliary, nonactivating style so it never steals focus from the app you are dragging from.
- The panel is an NSView that registers for .fileURL drag types. Dropped items are stored as security scoped bookmarks in memory plus a simple array model.
- Items render as a horizontal row of file icons from NSWorkspace.shared.icon, with filename labels and a count badge.
- The panel is also a drag source: implement NSDraggingSource and start a drag session on mouse down plus drag with the stored file URLs as NSPasteboardItems, so the files can be dragged into Finder, Mail, or any other app.
- Right click an item for Reveal in Finder, Open, Remove.
- Shake detection: use an NSEvent global monitor for leftMouseDragged, track direction reversals in a short rolling window, and if there are enough reversals within 600ms show the panel at the current cursor position. Guard the whole feature behind a user default so it can be turned off if the permission prompt is annoying.
- Persist nothing to disk. The shelf is cleared on quit.

Out of scope, do not build: cloud uploads, share links, AirDrop, multiple shelves, iCloud sync, analytics, accounts, auto update, any network calls at all.

No secrets are needed, so no .env. If you add any configuration, put it in UserDefaults.

Write a README that states exactly which parts are known fragile: file promise providers are not handled, so drags from browsers and Photos may produce empty drops, and shake detection requires Input Monitoring permission. Build it, run it, and confirm a Finder to shelf to Desktop round trip actually copies a file.
